LO 1 · Blood Pressure

Measure BP accurately, then interpret the number in context

The lecture's emphasis is that a blood-pressure number is only useful if the setup is valid. Technique errors can shift the reading by clinically meaningful amounts.

Prepare the room and patient. Quiet room; avoid caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, and exercise for at least 30 minutes; empty the bladder; rest 3–5 minutes without talking. No gum chewing.
Position correctly. Back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed, bare upper arm supported at heart level. Use an appropriately sized cuff.
Place the cuff. On the bare upper arm, about 2–3 cm above the elbow crease.
Read the sounds. The pressure at which you hear sounds from at least 2 consecutive beats is systolic BP. Continue deflating until the sounds muffle/disappear for diastolic BP.
Repeat. The slide recommends ≥2 measurements at least 30 seconds apart and averaging/recording them.
Positioning / behavior problemReading may be off by
Crossed legs2–8 mmHg
Cuff over clothing5–50 mmHg
Cuff too small2–10 mmHg
Full bladder10 mmHg
Talking or active listening10 mmHg
Unsupported arm10 mmHg
Unsupported back/feet6 mmHg
Interpretation boundary from this lecture: the deck teaches how to obtain a valid BP, but it does not provide hypertension staging thresholds. For a clinical scenario, first decide whether the measurement is technically trustworthy and use repeated/averaged values; do not invent a stage from this lecture alone.
Active recall: Why could a BP of 154/88 be misleading if the patient is talking, has a full bladder, and the arm is unsupported?
All three are listed measurement errors that can raise the measured pressure. The point is to fix technique and repeat/average rather than immediately treating one contaminated number as the patient's true BP.
LO 2 · Orthostatic Vital Signs

Recognize the 20/10 rule—and use the heart-rate response

Positive orthostatic BP change

Within 3 minutes of standing: sustained systolic drop ≥20 mmHg or diastolic drop ≥10 mmHg.

Symptoms matter

Postural dizziness, weakness, visual changes, or near-syncope are positive symptoms.

Expected normovolemic response

Approximate lecture values: HR ↑11 bpm, SBP ↓3.5 mmHg, DBP variable (about ↑5.2 mmHg).

Heart-rate clue

If HR fails to rise on standing, consider autonomic dysfunction. A postural pulse rise ≥30 bpm ± supine tachycardia correlates with hypovolemia in the cited McGee data.

Application example: supine 126/76, HR 70 → standing 102/66, HR 92 by 3 minutes. SBP falls 24 and DBP falls 10, so this meets the lecture definition of orthostatic hypotension. The HR rise is present rather than absent.
Memory hook: orthostatic hypotension = 20 / 10 / 3 → SBP 20, DBP 10, within 3 minutes.
Active recall: BP falls 24 mmHg systolic after standing, but HR does not increase. What extra concern does the lecture flag?
Autonomic dysfunction. The BP change meets orthostatic criteria; an inappropriate absent HR rise is the added clue.
LO 3 · JVD / HJR

Use the jugular vein as a bedside window into right-sided filling pressure

JVP setup

Head of bed 30–45°, tangential lighting. Observe the venous column's rise/fall and its waves/ascents/descents through respiration.

Jugular ≠ carotid

Jugular pulsation is not palpable, varies with inspiration/position, and can be altered by abdominal pressure. Carotid pulsation is palpable and does not behave that way.

Pressure conversion

Divide cm H2O by 1.36 to convert to mmHg. Lecture example: 11 cm H2O ≈ 8 mmHg.

Clinical pearl

If the JVP is visible while the patient is seated, the lecture gives an approximate JVP of ~10 cm.

Hepatojugular / abdominojugular reflux

Measure the baseline JVD/JVP.
Apply firm pressure of roughly 20–35 mmHg to the mid-abdomen for 15–30 seconds.
Keep the patient from tensing the abdomen or holding the breath.
Watch and re-measure the jugular venous column during compression.
Normal HJR: no rise, a transient rise <10 seconds, or a rise <4 cm H2O.
Positive HJR: the slide depicts a sustained rise ≥4 cm for ≥10 seconds. Causes listed: tricuspid regurgitation/right HF, constrictive/restrictive physiology, cardiac tamponade, IVC obstruction. It can predict HF when PCWP ≥15 mmHg.
Active recall: During abdominal compression the JVP rises 5 cm and stays elevated for 15 seconds. Normal or positive?
Positive HJR by the slide's threshold: sustained rise ≥4 cm for ≥10 seconds.
LO 4 · Cardiac Auscultation

Auscultate all 4 major posts + Erb's point with diaphragm and bell

Listening postLocation from LOWhat to deliberately assess
Aortic2nd ICS, right sternal borderS1/S2 relationship; systolic ejection murmur; radiation to neck if present
Pulmonic2nd ICS, left sternal borderS2/P2 and splitting; murmurs in the pulmonic area
Erb's pointLeft parasternal area between pulmonic and tricuspid listening regions (see lecture figure)Additional comparison point for heart sounds/murmurs
Tricuspid5th interspace, lower left sternal borderRight-sided sounds; holosystolic TR pattern if present
Mitral / apex5th ICS, midclavicular lineS1 is relatively prominent here; low-pitched S3/S4 are assessed best at apex in LLD with bell
At every post: state the rate and rhythm, identify S1/S2, and listen with both diaphragm and bell as the LO requires. If there is a murmur or gallop, do not stop at “murmur present”—characterize it.

Palpate for lifts, heaves, and thrills before you listen

Why this belongs here: the murmur grading table depends on whether a thrill is palpable, and the documentation example specifically notes “no palpable thrill.” Lifts/heaves are forceful precordial impulses; thrills are palpable vibrations from turbulent flow.

Describe a murmur using the lecture's SCRIPT

S — Site

Where is it loudest / point of maximum intensity?

C — Configuration

Crescendo, decrescendo, or both?

R — Radiation

Aortic → neck; mitral → axilla in the lecture.

I — Intensity

Grade it with the correct systolic or diastolic scale.

P — Pitch / Quality

Blowing, musical, harsh, rumbling, honking, whooping, buzzing, etc.

T — Timing

Systolic, diastolic, continuous; specify early/mid/late/holo when appropriate.

Presentation / documentation examples

NORMAL: “Cardiac exam: rate 72 beats/min, regular rhythm. S1 and S2 normal. No murmurs or gallops appreciated.” ABNORMAL EXAMPLE: “Cardiac exam: regular rate and rhythm. Grade 3/6 mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur, maximal at the aortic area with radiation to the neck; no palpable thrill.”
Active recall: Why is “3/6 murmur” incomplete documentation?
Because the lecture expects site, configuration, radiation, intensity, pitch/quality, and timing—plus rate/rhythm and associated sounds.
LO 5 · Heart Sounds

Distinguish S1, S2, S2 splitting, S3, and S4

SoundTiming / mechanismBest heardLecture interpretationHook
S1Mitral + tricuspid closure; onset of systoleHigh pitched, diaphragm; loudest at apexSplitting is unusual/possibly abnormal; examples listed include RBBB, atrial myxoma, Ebstein anomaly“Lub”
S2Aortic + pulmonic closure; end systole / beginning diastoleHigh pitched, diaphragm; 2nd–3rd interspaces near left sternumPhysiologic split widens with inspiration and narrows/joins with expiration“Dub”
S3Early diastole; rapid inflow into a compliant ventricle / volume striking ventricular wallApex, left lateral decubitus, bellCan be normal in young people, athletes, pregnancy; pathologic associations include HF/LV dysfunction, valvular disease, dilated cardiomyopathyKentucky
S4Late diastole; atrial contraction into non-compliant LVApex, left lateral decubitus, bellLecture labels it always abnormal; associated with LVH + CAD; absent in AF because atrial contraction is requiredTennessee

S2 splitting

Physiologic

A2 and P2 separate during inspiration and come together during expiration. Inspiration lowers pulmonary vascular impedance and increases RV filling, prolonging RV ejection.

Fixed

Split during both inspiration and expiration. The lecture's classic association is ASD.

Paradoxical — lecture wording

The supplied slide labels expiratory splitting as “paradoxical” and lists RBBB or pulmonary hypertension. This is reproduced as presented in the deck.

Active recall: Why is an S4 absent in atrial fibrillation?
S4 requires active atrial contraction into a non-compliant ventricle; atrial fibrillation removes coordinated atrial contraction.

Mid-diastolic↑ flow or obstruction across mitral/tricuspid valvesMR/MS/TR/TS or ASD
PresystolicLate diastole coinciding with atrial contractionMS/TS or atrial myxoma

Active recall: A moderate systolic murmur without a palpable thrill is what grade?
Grade 3/6. A palpable thrill first appears in the lecture's grade 4 systolic definition.
LO 7 · Clubbing, Cyanosis, Edema

Describe the abnormal finding first, then connect it to the differential

Clubbing

Recognize it

Loss of the normal nail-fold angle / increased Lovibond profile angle, progressive bulbous distal digit, and loss of the normal Schamroth window.

Pulmonary causes shown

Bronchial carcinoma, fibrosing alveolitis, chronic suppurative disease (empyema, abscess, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis), mesothelioma.

Cardiac causes shown

Congenital cyanotic heart disease, endocarditis, atrial myxoma.

GI / other causes shown

Cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, GI lymphoma; familial and thyroid acropachy are also listed.

Cyanosis

PatternLecture mnemonicCauses shown
PeripheralCOLDCold; Obstruction; LV failure and shock; Decreased cardiac output
CentralPALMSPolycythemia; Altitude; Lung disease; Methemoglobinemia; Shunt

Edema

GradeDepth / persistence on lecture slide
0+No pitting
1+~2 mm depression, disappears rapidly
2+~4 mm, disappears in 10–15 seconds
3+~6 mm, may persist >1 minute
4+~8 mm, may persist >2 minutes
HF-associated edema in the case packet: typically dependent and pitting, often bilateral ± asymmetric. But edema is not specific for HF—the case packet emphasizes that it is common in both cardiac and non-cardiac conditions. The lecture also displays May–Thurner syndrome and lymphedema as alternative edema patterns.
Active recall: Which cyanosis mnemonic belongs to central causes?
PALMS: polycythemia, altitude, lung disease, methemoglobinemia, shunt.

Arterial vs venous ulcers are directly covered; three LO categories require a labeled supplement

FeatureArterial disease / ulcerVenous disease / ulcer
SitePressure points; metatarsal heads, heel, lateral malleolusGaiter area / ankle, especially medial malleolus

Source boundary: the supplied Segal cardiac exam lecture directly illustrates and compares arterial and venous ulcer disease. Searchable text in the uploaded deck does not provide neurotrophic/neuropathic, traumatic, or malignant ulcer teaching. The three entries below are therefore a clearly labeled general-medical-knowledge supplement added only because those categories appear in your LO; they should not be attributed to Dr. Segal's slides.
Supplemental category — not in supplied deckTypical distinguishing patternHigh-yield clue
Neurotrophic / neuropathicOften at repetitive pressure-bearing points, commonly plantar; may be deep with surrounding callus and relatively little pain because sensation is impaired.Neuropathy + pressure point + callus + reduced pain.
TraumaticDistribution and shape follow the mechanism of injury (pressure, friction, laceration, burn, etc.); pain and depth are variable.A convincing local injury/mechanical history fits the lesion.
MalignantChronic nonhealing or changing ulcer may develop induration, everted/rolled irregular edges, friability, exuberant tissue, or bleeding.Persistent/atypical ulcer → malignancy must be considered and tissue diagnosis is required clinically.
Active recall: Medial-malleolar, large, shallow, irregular ulcer with stasis dermatitis and intact pulses—arterial or venous?
Venous. Arterial ulcers in the lecture are more often small/deep “punched out” lesions at pressure points with weak/absent pulses.
LO 9 · Ischemia / ACS / AMI / CHF

Use history + exam findings as diagnostic weights—not binary rules

Cardiac ischemia / ACS / AMI: history features that increase suspicion

History component from case packetHow it shifts suspicion
Central/retrosternal pressure, squeezing, gripping, heaviness, tightness; exertional/stress-relatedHigher suspicion in the lecture's probability graphic
Sharp / fleeting / shifting / pleuritic / positional painLower suspicion; the deck also notes sharp + stabbing descriptors more powerfully separate non-ischemic from ischemic pain
Radiation to right arm/shoulderLR+ 4.7 in the cited review
Radiation to both arms/shouldersLR+ 4.1
Associated with exertionLR+ 2.4
Radiation to left armLR+ 2.3
DiaphoresisLR+ 2.0
Nausea or vomitingLR+ 1.9
Worse than prior angina / similar to prior MILR+ 1.8
Described as pressureLR+ 1.3
Do not overvalue gestures. Levine/palm/arm/pointing signs all had low sensitivity in the case packet. Pointing was presented as a non-ischemic indicator, while larger chest-pain diameter was associated with 2.2× higher odds of a positive troponin.

SymptomLecture meaning / mechanismDiagnostic weight shown

FindingCase-packet diagnostic weightTakeaway

Integrated bedside presentation: “Progressive exertional dyspnea with orthopnea/PND, elevated JVP, positive HJR, and an S3” is a much stronger HF pattern than edema alone. Likewise, ACS/AMI suspicion should come from the entire chest-pain pattern, radiation, associated symptoms, risk history, and objective evaluation—not a single descriptor or gesture.
Active recall: Which of the listed HF physical findings has the strongest LR+ in the case packet?
S3, approximately LR+ 11.4 in the displayed evidence-based exam table. JVP and abdominojugular reflux also carry meaningful positive weight.
Week 5 Cardiovascular

High-Yield LO One-Pager

LO1 · Blood Pressure — measure, apply, interpret

  • Prep: quiet room, no caffeine/nicotine/exercise ×30 min, empty bladder, rest 3–5 min without talking.
  • Position: back/feet supported, legs uncrossed, bare arm supported at heart level, correct cuff size 2–3 cm above the antecubital crease.
  • Read: SBP = sound at ≥2 consecutive beats; DBP = sounds muffle/disappear.
  • Repeat ≥2× ≥30 sec apart, average.
  • Error → shift: cuff over clothing 5–50 mmHg; full bladder 10; talking 10; unsupported arm 10; unsupported back/feet 6; crossed legs 2–8; wrong cuff size 2–10.
  • Apply/interpret: before treating a number as real, confirm technique was valid and use the averaged, repeated reading — this lecture gives technique, not HTN staging cutoffs.

LO2 · Orthostatic Vitals — measure, apply, interpret

  • How: supine BP/HR after rest, then repeat within 3 min of standing.
  • Positive (20/10/3): SBP ↓≥20 or DBP ↓≥10 mmHg within 3 min standing; symptoms (dizziness, weakness, visual change, near-syncope) support it.
  • Expected normal response: HR ↑~11, SBP ↓~3.5, DBP ~↑5.2.
  • Interpret the HR response: no compensatory HR rise → think autonomic dysfunction; HR rise ≥30 bpm ± supine tachycardia → clue for hypovolemia.
  • Applied: 126/76 HR 70 supine → 102/66 HR 92 standing = SBP −24/DBP −10 (positive) with an appropriate HR rise → favors volume-mediated over autonomic cause.

LO3 · JVD & HJR — evaluate and interpret

  • JVP setup: HOB 30–45°, tangential light; jugular pulsation is non-palpable, biphasic, varies with respiration/position (vs. carotid: palpable, doesn't vary).
  • Measure/convert: vertical height above sternal angle; cm H₂O ÷1.36 = mmHg (11 cm ≈ 8 mmHg); JVP visible while seated ≈10 cm.
  • Interpret elevated JVP: ↑ right atrial/central venous pressure — right HF, TR, constrictive/restrictive physiology, tamponade, SVC/IVC obstruction.
  • HJR technique: firm 20–35 mmHg mid-abdominal pressure ×15–30 sec; patient breathes normally, doesn't strain.
  • Interpret: normal = no rise, or rise <4 cm and/or resolves <10 sec. Positive = sustained rise ≥4 cm for ≥10 sec → right HF/TR, constrictive/tamponade physiology, IVC obstruction; can predict PCWP ≥15 mmHg.

LO4 · Auscultation — posts, technique, documentation

  • 4 posts + Erb's: Aortic 2nd ICS RSB · Pulmonic 2nd ICS LSB · Erb's point (between pulmonic/tricuspid) · Tricuspid 5th ICS LLSB · Mitral/apex 5th ICS MCL.
  • Use diaphragm (high-pitched: S1, S2, most murmurs) and bell (low-pitched: S3, S4, MS rumble) at every post.
  • Sequence: state rate + rhythm → identify S1/S2 → screen for extra sounds/murmurs/gallops → if present, fully characterize (SCRIPT below) → link finding to a disease process.
  • SCRIPT: Site, Configuration, Radiation, Intensity (grade), Pitch/quality, Timing.
  • Document — normal: "Rate 72, regular rhythm. S1/S2 normal. No murmurs or gallops." Abnormal: "Regular rate/rhythm. Grade 3/6 mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur, maximal at the aortic area, radiates to the neck, no thrill."

LO5 · Heart Sounds — S1, S2, splitting, S3, S4

  • S1 "Lub": mitral+tricuspid closure, onset of systole; loudest apex, diaphragm.
  • S2 "Dub": aortic+pulmonic closure, end systole/onset diastole; loudest base, diaphragm.
  • Physiologic split: widens with inspiration (↓intrathoracic pressure → ↑RV filling → delays P2), narrows/fuses with expiration.
  • Fixed split: present equally in inspiration and expiration → classic for ASD.
  • Paradoxical split (as taught): reversed pattern, widens on expiration → RBBB, pulmonary hypertension.
  • S3 "Kentucky": early diastole, rapid filling into a compliant/volume-loaded ventricle; apex, LLD, bell. Can be normal (young/athlete/pregnancy) or pathologic (HF, valve disease, dilated cardiomyopathy).
  • S4 "Tennessee": late diastole, atrial kick into a stiff LV (LVH/CAD); apex, LLD, bell. Always abnormal; absent in AF (needs organized atrial contraction).

LO6 · Systolic vs. Diastolic Murmurs — compare and grade

  • Systolic: holosystolic = constant gradient → MR/TR. Mid-systolic crescendo–decrescendo = ejection → AS. Early systolic (starts with S1) → acute MR/TR w/o pulm HTN. Late systolic, high-pitched → MVP ± click, ischemic MR.
  • Diastolic: early, decrescendo, starts at S2 → AR. Mid-diastolic (↑flow/obstruction across AV valves) → MS/MR/TR/TS/ASD. Presystolic (coincides with atrial kick) → MS/TS or atrial myxoma.
  • Systolic grade 1–6: 1 barely audible → 2 slight → 3 moderate, no thrill → 4 loud + palpable thrill → 5 very loud, thrill easily felt → 6 audible off the chest.
  • Diastolic grade 1–4: 1 very soft → 2 soft → 3 moderate → 4 loud/thrill.

LO7 · Clubbing, Cyanosis, Edema — findings + causes

  • Clubbing: ↑nail-fold (Lovibond) angle, bulbous distal digit, loss of Schamroth's window. Causes: pulmonary (bronchial CA, fibrosing alveolitis, chronic suppuration/bronchiectasis/CF/empyema, mesothelioma); cardiac (cyanotic CHD, endocarditis, atrial myxoma); GI/other (cirrhosis, IBD, celiac, GI lymphoma, thyroid acropachy).
  • Cyanosis — peripheral = COLD: Cold exposure, Obstruction (arterial/venous), LV failure/shock, Decreased cardiac output. Central = PALMS: Polycythemia, Altitude, Lung disease, Methemoglobinemia, Shunt (R→L).
  • Edema: grade 0–4+ by pitting depth/recovery time. HF edema is typically bilateral, dependent, pitting — but nonspecific; also seen with venous insufficiency, lymphedema, May–Thurner, hypoalbuminemia, and medications.

LO8 · Lower-Extremity Ulcers — arterial vs. venous vs. neurotrophic vs. traumatic vs. malignant

  • Arterial: pressure points/toes/heel; small, deep, "punched-out," regular border; pale/dry base, little drainage; painful; cool skin, cap refill >3s, weak/absent pulses; minimal edema.
  • Venous: medial gaiter/malleolus; large, shallow, irregular border; moist/granulating, heavy drainage; typically painless; warm, stasis dermatitis/hyperpigmentation, intact pulses; edema + varicosities present.
  • Neurotrophic: plantar/pressure-bearing points in a neuropathic foot; deep with surrounding callus; little pain (impaired sensation) — key clue is neuropathy + pressure point + callus.
  • Traumatic: shape/location follows the injury mechanism (pressure, friction, laceration, burn); variable pain/depth; history of a matching local injury.
  • Malignant: chronic, nonhealing, or changing ulcer with everted/rolled or irregular edges, induration, friability, or bleeding → biopsy for tissue diagnosis.

LO9 · History/Exam Features → Ischemia, ACS, AMI, CHF

  • ↑ suspicion for ischemia/ACS/AMI: central/retrosternal pressure, squeezing, heaviness, exertional trigger. LR+: right-arm radiation 4.7, both-arm radiation 4.1, exertional 2.4, left-arm radiation 2.3, diaphoresis 2.0, nausea/vomiting 1.9, worse-than-prior-angina/like-prior-MI 1.8, described as pressure 1.3. Larger pain area → 2.2× higher odds of positive troponin.
  • ↓ suspicion: sharp/fleeting/shifting/pleuritic/positional pain. Levine sign/palm/arm-pointing gestures have low sensitivity — don't overweight them.
  • CHF history (LR+): PND ~2.6, orthopnea ~2.2, edema ~2.1 (nonspecific), DOE ~1.3; bendopnea flags advanced HF/low cardiac index.
  • CHF exam (LR+): S3 ~11.4 (strongest, spec ~0.99), displaced apical impulse lateral to MCL (10.3 for low EF, 13.0 for CAD, 5.8 for ↑filling pressure), HJR/AJR ~6.4, JVD ~5.1 (JVP ≥12 mmHg = highest PPV), crackles ~2.8, any murmur ~2.6, LE edema ~2.3 (nonspecific).
  • Integrate the full pattern (history + exam) rather than any single finding or gesture when weighing ischemia/ACS/AMI vs. CHF.
